newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Australia sees A$14 bln gas investment to 2005.
newsitem.headline: Australia sees A$14 bln gas investment to 2005.

text.p: A rapidly-expanding gas market in Australia will require capital investment of at least A$14 billion (US$10.8 billion) up to the year 2005, the Australian Gas Association (AGA) said on Monday.
The AGA, releasing a report into gas supply and demand which forecasts a trebling of natural gas consumption to the year 2030, said A$3 billion was needed for proposed pipelines alone.

AGA chief executive Ian Woodward said the study, released at a gas conference here, demonstrated Australia had sufficient gas resource capability to meet accelerating demand, provided new multi-billion dollar pipeline and field investments were made.
This was especially critical for eastern Australia to have sufficient gas available early next century, he said.
The study forecasts increasing interstate gas trade, new pipelines, additional exploration and the creation of an integrated pipeline grid, Woodward said.

Long-term supply options for eastern Australia, to augment locally available gas, include using some gas reserves from Western Australia, the Northern Territory and Papua New Guinea. These options would be considered next decade, Woodward said.
The study showed that national gas industry reform was the key to facilitating new investments and stimulating the market.

If private infrastructure was to meet demand, governments, consumers and gas industry players would have to agree to the content of and definitive timetable for access reforms, Woodward said. "(1997) is crunch time for gas reform decisions," he said.

Natural gas would be Australia's fastest-growing energy source to year 2030, with average annual projected growth of about three percent leading to gas raising its national primary energy share to more than 28 percent from 18 percent, he told the conference.
Reform to achieve free and fair gas trade, including national open access, had to be finalised urgently, he said.
Investment requirements represented a minimum 40 percent annual increase in direct spending over current levels, he said.
